title: Trump Orders Steam Catapults Back on Ford-Class Carriers and a Fifth Public Shipyard; AEVEX Buys BlackSea for $650M
subhead: A National Security Presidential Memorandum orders the Navy to drop EMALS for steam catapults on future Ford-class carriers and establishes a fifth public shipyard for submarine repair, while AEVEX moves to acquire naval autonomy firm BlackSea Technologies for up to $650 million.

sections.heading: Navy Ordered Back to Steam: Carrier Catapults and a New Public Shipyard
sections.body:
President Donald Trump signed a National Security Presidential Memorandum today ordering the return of steam-powered catapults and hydraulic elevators to Ford-class aircraft carriers, along with the establishment of a fifth public shipyard for submarine repair and a new component repair center to cut submarine delays, a White House official confirmed to Breaking Defense. The memo directs Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to deliver a readiness plan within 120 days covering both the private sector and the additional yard.

The change targets the Electromagnetic Aircraft Launch System (EMALS) used on the lead ship USS Ford, which Trump has long criticized. Future carriers such as the Doris Miller under construction at HII's Newport News Shipbuilding would revert to the steam and hydraulic systems used on Nimitz-class ships. General Atomics, EMALS' builder, warned that with 'nearly 50% of production complete,' reversing course 'would introduce significant cost, schedule, and integration risks.'
sections.whyItMatters: This is a major industrial reversal: the Navy has not bought a steam catapult in more than two decades, so suppliers would need to rebuild production lines from scratch even as the service wrestles with submarine and carrier maintenance backlogs. Hudson Institute's Bryan Clark notes restoring steam lines to the catapults 'will require extensive redesign of the ship' on a class already well into construction.

sections.heading: AEVEX to Acquire BlackSea Technologies for Up to $650M
sections.body:
Defense tech firm AEVEX announced Wednesday it is acquiring naval technology company BlackSea Technologies for up to $650 million, a deal slated to close in September. Breaking Defense reports the transaction includes $250 million in cash, roughly $350 million in AEVEX Class A common stock, and up to $50 million in performance-based earnout. The goal is to expand AEVEX's footprint in unmanned surface and undersea vessels and deepen 'customer access' to the Navy, US Special Operations Command and allied partners.

BlackSea builds the Global Autonomous Reconnaissance Craft (GARC), a 16-foot autonomous vessel operated by the Navy's Unmanned Surface Vessel Squadron 3 out of Naval Base Coronado. AEVEX, based in Solana Beach, California, fields its own autonomous systems including the Mako unmanned surface vessel for ISR and kinetic operations.
sections.whyItMatters: The deal is a consolidation play in the fast-growing unmanned maritime sector, pairing AEVEX's air-and-surface portfolio with BlackSea's deployed naval reconnaissance craft at a moment when the Navy is standing up dedicated robotic and autonomous systems commands.

sections.heading: Poland Launches First Miecznik-Class Frigate
sections.body:
Poland launched ORP Wicher, the first of three multi-role frigates under its Miecznik modernization program, into Gdansk Bay on Thursday. The roughly $4 billion program, attended by President Karol Nawrocki and Prime Minister Donald Tusk, will replace Poland's obsolete Oliver Hazard Perry-class ships and form the backbone of its surface strike force, with missions spanning air defense, anti-submarine warfare and protection of critical infrastructure like the Baltic Pipe gas line.

Wicher is slated for delivery in 2029, with the second frigate ORP Burza launching in September 2027 and the third, ORP Huragan, begun in April. Tusk framed the program as 'a real strengthening of Baltic security,' and Nawrocki cited Russia's Baltic Fleet and Kaliningrad as the strategic rationale. The ships are built by Poland's PGZ consortium under the Miecznik effort launched in 2021.
sections.whyItMatters: The launch is a tangible milestone in Eastern Europe's post-2022 naval rearmament, rebuilding domestic shipbuilding capacity and Baltic presence against Russia while Europe funds its own frigate production lines rather than buying off the shelf.

sections.heading: C4ADS Documents Russian Air Bridge to the Sahel: 75 Flights
sections.body:
A new Center for Advanced Defense Studies (C4ADS) analysis, reported by Defense News, found Russian state-aligned military forces relied on at least 75 flights by military and military-linked aircraft into the Central Sahel between January 2025 and July 2026, based on ADS-B flight-tracking data covering Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger. Burkina Faso received the most flights at 56, followed by Mali at 38 and Niger at six.

The busiest operator was Flight Unit 224, a Russian Defense Ministry-owned airline sanctioned by the US in May 2023. State aircraft typically refueled at Russia's Khmeimim air base in Syria and Libyan sites before continuing south, while private carriers transited UAE, Algerian and Turkish hubs. C4ADS flagged private carriers such as Sapsan Airlines as still unsanctioned despite documented links to Russian military logistics.
sections.whyItMatters: The sustained air bridge underscores Russia's deepening logistics footprint in the Sahel and West Africa, where Moscow has displaced French and Western forces — evidence of an increasingly routinized military support network that sanctions have only partially disrupted.

sections.heading: Boeing Pitches an Ultra Low-Cost Seeker to Lower Weapon Prices
sections.body:
Boeing unveiled its Ultra Low-Cost Seeker (ULCS) at this week's Space and Missile Defense Symposium in Huntsville, an active radar seeker built largely from commercial off-the-shelf parts adapted for military use. Seekers are among the most expensive components of a guided weapon, and Boeing's argument — reported by Defense News — is that seeker cost is what limits how many weapons the military can buy. The design is intended to be reusable across interceptors, guided bombs and cruise missiles rather than requiring a separate seeker for each.

Boeing said the ULCS completed several tests this summer, including anechoic-chamber checks, captive-carry flights aboard a Beechcraft 1900 over land and water, and a live launch at Spaceport America where the seeker tracked and hit a drone target. Bob Ciesla, a Boeing vice president, said the goal is 'sharing a common sensor architecture across several of our programs.'
sections.whyItMatters: Affordability is the binding constraint on missile and munition stockpiles — a theme running through the Pentagon's production acceleration push. A cheap, reusable seeker directly attacks that constraint and could reshape how many guided weapons the US can buy and sustain.

sections.heading: DARPA Wants a Next-Generation Hypersonic Cruise Missile
sections.body:
DARPA has issued a Request for Information for a Next Generation Hypersonic Cruise Missile (NGHCM), a scramjet-powered weapon designed to evade increasingly capable enemy Integrated Air Defense Systems, Defense News reports. The RFI, due October 6, calls for a demonstrator that is both survivable and affordable enough to be manufactured in large quantities, explicitly encouraging bids from 'non-traditional defense contractors and emerging technology developers.'

DARPA frames the need in terms of peer adversaries proliferating advanced air defenses that 'threaten to restrict the operational freedom of U.S. forces.' The RFI asks industry to weigh trade-offs among payload, range, speed and altitude against signature and maneuverability, and to consider launch platforms from tactical fighters and heavy bombers to ground-based vertical launch systems.
sections.whyItMatters: Hypersonic strike is converging with the affordability push: DARPA is signaling that the next leap is not just speed but producibility at scale, a deliberate effort to keep US stand-off strike viable against denser air-defense networks.

sections.heading: Golden Dome Moves Forward: Interceptor Milestone and Army Air-Defense Unit
sections.body: The Pentagon's Golden Dome missile-defense push advanced on multiple fronts this week. Gen. Michael Guetlein said at the Space and Missile Defense Symposium that space-based interceptor contractors have passed the first program milestone, though the Defense Department will not decide on producing operational space-based interceptors until industry demonstrates feasibility, per Breaking Defense. Separately, the Army selected an air-defense unit to prepare for the Golden Dome mission, with Lt. Gen. John Rafferty saying the service will experiment and test with the unit ahead of a 2028 delivery.
sections.whyItMatters: Golden Dome is transitioning from concept to concrete programmatic steps — feasibility gates for space interceptors and a designated Army unit to operate the capability — even as funding questions around the layered architecture remain unresolved.

bottomLine: The signature development of the day is a US naval-industrial reversal: Trump ordered future Ford-class carriers back to steam catapults and hydraulics and directed a fifth public shipyard for submarine repair, overruling General Atomics' warning about sunk costs — a decision that will ripple through carrier design, supplier base and readiness for years. Around it, the defense market stayed busy: AEVEX is consolidating unmanned maritime capability with a $650M BlackSea acquisition, Poland floated the first Miecznik frigate to rebuild its Baltic fleet, C4ADS quantified a 75-flight Russian air bridge into the Sahel, and both Boeing and DARPA pushed affordability-first approaches to seekers and hypersonic strike. The through-line across the day is cost and industrial capacity: Western navies and missile programs are all trying to solve the same problem of producing and sustaining more capability at scale, even as strategic posture shifts in the Baltic, the Sahel and the Indo-Pacific.
sources: Breaking Defense, Defense News, Center for Advanced Defense Studies (C4ADS), The Wall Street Journal
